title: Recommender Fundamentals
summary: Frame recommendation as predicting a user-item preference, and understand the cold-start problem every approach has to work around.

slides.markdown:
A **recommender system** predicts how much a user will like an item they haven't interacted with yet, then ranks items by that prediction. Think of it as a matchmaker: given everything you've watched, bought, or clicked, it guesses what you'd want next — and every home feed, "you might also like" rail, and playlist mix is one running live.

- Input: a **user**, a set of **candidate items**, and history of interactions.
- Output: a **score** or **rank** over candidates, not a single yes/no.
- The hard part is rarely the algorithm — it's getting honest signal about what "liked" even means.

slides.subTitle: What are we actually predicting?
slides.markdown:
Formally, a recommender learns a function `score(user, item) → relevance`, then returns the top-k items by that score for a given user. "Relevance" is a proxy — usually predicted probability of a click, watch, purchase, or rating.

The catalog and user base are both huge (millions of items, millions of users), so the interesting engineering problem is **scoring only plausible candidates fast**, not scoring every item for every user. This is why production systems split into candidate generation and ranking — a preview of the multi-stage funnel covered later in this group.

Feedback comes in two flavors, and which one you have shapes everything downstream:

- **Explicit feedback** — the user deliberately tells you: a 5-star rating, a thumbs up, a review. Clean signal, but rare — most users never rate anything.
- **Implicit feedback** — inferred from behavior: clicks, watch-time, add-to-cart, dwell time, skips. Abundant, but noisy and one-sided — you see what a user *did*, never what they'd have rated something they never saw.

In practice, almost every large-scale recommender (Netflix, YouTube, Amazon) is trained mostly on implicit feedback, because it's the only signal available at scale.

**Cold start** is what happens when there's no interaction history to learn from, and it comes in two shapes:

- **New user** — you have zero clicks/ratings for them, so any personalization is a guess. Systems fall back to popularity, onboarding surveys, or demographic priors until enough history accumulates.
- **New item** — a freshly-uploaded video or listing has no engagement yet, so collaborative signals ("users who liked X also liked Y") can't see it at all. Content-based signals (title, tags, image embeddings) are the only way to surface it early.

Cold start isn't a bug to patch once — it's a permanent, ongoing fraction of traffic in any growing product.

The two foundational approaches use fundamentally different signal:

| Approach | Signal used | Cold-start weakness |
|---|---|---|
| Content-based | Item features (genre, tags, text) matched to a user's own history | New user with no history |
| Collaborative filtering | Patterns across *all* users' interactions | New item with no interactions |

**How to decide:** collaborative filtering usually wins on raw accuracy once you have volume, because it captures taste patterns no feature engineer would think to encode — but almost every real system blends both (hybrid, covered later) precisely to cover each other's cold-start gap.

slides.subTitle: "More data" doesn't fix a blank slate
slides.markdown:
A common mistake: assuming that because the *platform* has huge data, cold start is basically solved. It isn't. A brand-new user with zero clicks has the exact same problem on a platform with a billion interactions as on one with a thousand — collaborative filtering has nothing to key off *for that user*, no matter how much data exists for everyone else.

The fix is architectural, not volume: onboarding flows that elicit a few preferences upfront, popularity/trending fallbacks, and content-based signals for the first several sessions until behavioral data accumulates.

slides.subTitle: Precision@k and recall@k on a top-5 list
slides.markdown:
Say a user actually likes 8 items in the catalog, and a recommender's top-5 list contains 3 of them. **Precision@5** asks "of what we showed, how much was relevant": `3/5 = 0.6`. **Recall@5** asks "of what's relevant, how much did we surface": `3/8 = 0.375`.

These pull in different directions: a list of 1 correct item out of 1 shown has perfect precision (1.0) but poor recall; showing every single catalog item would have perfect recall (1.0) but terrible precision. Recommenders care most about precision at small k (position 1-5 dominates what a user actually sees), while recall matters more when evaluating the earlier candidate-generation stage, whose whole job is not to miss relevant items before ranking even gets a chance to see them.

slides.subTitle: Serendipity, coverage, and diversity as quality dimensions
slides.markdown:
A recommender that's perfectly accurate by every precision/recall metric can still be a poor product if it only ever resurfaces the same obvious, popular items to everyone. Three additional dimensions matter in practice: **serendipity** — surfacing something the user wouldn't have found on their own but genuinely enjoys, not just the safest, most-predictable match; **coverage** — what fraction of the catalog ever gets recommended to anyone (a system that only ever shows the top 1% of items has poor coverage, no matter how accurate); **diversity** — how varied a single user's recommendation list is, versus near-duplicates of the same thing.

These dimensions often trade off against raw accuracy — the single most "accurate" recommendation is frequently the safest, most obvious one — which is why production systems explicitly track and optimize for them rather than assuming accuracy alone captures product quality.

slides.subTitle: Optimizing rating-prediction accuracy doesn't guarantee good rankings
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "If our model achieves low RMSE predicting the exact rating a user would give an item, it will naturally produce a great recommendation list."

**Why it's wrong:** RMSE rewards getting every prediction close to its true value across the *whole* ratings range, but users only ever see the **top of the ranked list** — a model can have excellent RMSE while getting the relative order of the top 10 items wrong (e.g. consistently underestimating 4.5-star items relative to 4.7-star ones by exactly the same small amount doesn't hurt RMSE much, but can invert which one a user sees first).

**Correct model:** evaluate with a ranking-aware metric (precision@k, NDCG) that specifically measures whether the *top* of the list is right, since that's the only part of the output a real user ever actually experiences — a rating-prediction-accuracy metric like RMSE is a reasonable proxy during model development but isn't the same objective as producing a good top-k list.
